record.original_question: Can one develop a perturbation theory for non-solvable KPZ-type interacting-particle models that plays a role analogous to KAM theory in integrable dynamical systems, so that persistence of integrability-like structure and robustness of asymptotic scaling phenomena can be studied beyond exactly solvable models?

evidence.quote: In addition, it is particularly frustrating that there is no known perturbation theory, analogous to KAM theory for integrable dynamical systems, that one can use to investigate the persistence of "integrability" for non-solvable models and demonstrate robustness for asymptotic scaling phenomena. Developing such a perturbation theory is an open conceptual and technical problem of the first order.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Develop a perturbation theory for KPZ-type interacting-particle systems (one-dimensional stochastic growth and interacting-particle models in the Kardar–Parisi–Zhang universality class, such as asymmetric exclusion processes, last-passage percolation, polymer models, and corner growth models) that plays the role analogous to Kolmogorov–Arnold–Moser (KAM) theory in classical integrable Hamiltonian dynamics. Specifically, construct a rigorous framework with the following features:

(a) Starting from an exactly solvable ("integrable") KPZ-type model whose one-point distributions, correlation functions, and scaling limits (e.g. Tracy–Widom fluctuations with exponent 1/3 and spatial scale 2/3) are known exactly via determinantal/Bethe-ansatz structures, identify a quantitative notion of "integrable structure" (e.g. determinantal correlation kernels, Markov dualities, intertwiners, or algebraic symmetries) that can be tracked under small perturbations of the model's transition rates or local interactions.

(b) Prove that, for sufficiently small but non-trivial perturbations that destroy exact solvability, a portion of this integrable structure persists in a controlled (possibly asymptotic) sense.

(c) Use this persistence to deduce, rigorously, that the perturbed (non-solvable) model still lies in the KPZ universality class — i.e. that its large-time fluctuations, after appropriate centering and rescaling, converge to the KPZ fixed point (or, on intermediate scales, to the KPZ equation), with the same scaling exponents and limiting distributions as the unperturbed solvable model.

The problem is to either produce such a perturbation theory together with a class of non-solvable models for which universality can be derived from solvable ones, or to establish fundamental obstructions ruling out such a theory.
artifact.status_search_result: No KAM-style perturbation theory for KPZ-type non-solvable interacting-particle models is known. Surveys and lecture notes on the KPZ universality class (Corwin, Quastel, Baik, Petrov) continue to emphasize that universality is rigorously established only for special solvable models and certain weak-asymmetry/intermediate disorder limits, with no general framework for perturbing away from integrable models. The problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Kardar-Parisi-Zhang Universality (Corwin)
status_evidence.snippet: The KPZ equation has only been shown to rigorously occur as the scaling limit of a few special models, for example, weakly asymmetric simple exclusion processes, and weakly rescaled polymers.
status_evidence.claim: Rigorous KPZ universality is restricted to special (solvable or weakly perturbed) models, indicating absence of a general perturbation theory.

status_evidence.title: KPZ limit theorems (Baik, ICM)
status_evidence.snippet: Survey of KPZ limit theorems primarily for integrable/solvable models.
status_evidence.claim: State-of-the-art results still rely on exact solvability rather than a perturbative framework.

status_evidence.title: Introduction to KPZ (Quastel)
status_evidence.snippet: Discussion of solvable models and the lack of techniques for non-solvable perturbations.
status_evidence.claim: No KAM-analog perturbation theory is presented; non-solvable models remain out of reach.
